title: Isomerism in Organic Chemistry

references.label: NCERT Chemistry Part II, Class 11 — Organic Chemistry: Some Basic Principles and Techniques

summary: Isomers are compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures (structural isomerism) or different spatial arrangements (stereoisomerism).
explanation: Structural isomers differ in how atoms are connected: chain isomerism (different carbon skeleton branching), position isomerism (same skeleton, functional group at a different position), and functional group isomerism (same formula, entirely different functional groups, e.g. an alcohol and an ether). Stereoisomers have identical connectivity but differ in 3D spatial arrangement: geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism arises from restricted rotation (e.g. around a double bond), while optical isomerism arises from chirality (a molecule and its non-superimposable mirror image, typically due to a carbon attached to four different groups).
commonMisconceptions: Confusing functional group isomers (completely different chemical behavior, e.g. ethanol vs dimethyl ether, both C₂H₆O) with position isomers (same functional group, same general reactivity, different location).
Assuming any molecule with a double bond shows cis-trans isomerism — it requires each carbon of the double bond to have two DIFFERENT substituents.
examples: Ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) and dimethyl ether (CH₃OCH₃) are functional group isomers, both with molecular formula C₂H₆O but completely different properties.
genZNote: Isomers are chemistry's way of saying 'same ingredients, different recipe' — the atoms are identical, but how they're arranged changes everything about the molecule's personality.
